pron_note: Two syllables, not three — the -eyed collapses to "-need," never "hack-NEE-id."
means:
Worn out by repetition; so overused it has lost all force. Said of **phrases, plots, themes, jokes, arguments** — the things that get repeated.

The charge isn't that the thing is *wrong* — it's that it was once effective and has been ridden into the ground. "Love conquers all" isn't false; it's hackneyed. Note also who says it: this is a reviewer's word, dry and faintly superior, the verdict of someone who has read too many manuscripts. *Cliché* just labels the phrase; **hackneyed** convicts the writer of laziness.
trick_line: Sitting right inside it is **hack** — and a hack is a writer with no fresh lines left.
trick_unpack: Same word, same origin: hackneyed prose is hack work, which is why the insult lands on the writer and not just the sentence.
sentences: The reviewer dismissed the novel's central metaphor as **hackneyed**, a device already exhausted by a generation of imitators.
Every best-man speech uses the same **hackneyed** joke about the groom finally being off the market.
etymology:
From **Hackney**, once a village outside London where horses were pastured and **let out for hire**. A *hackney* was the rental horse — ridden by anyone who paid, and worn out by all of them.

That single image gives you the whole family: **hack** (a writer for hire, churning out the same stuff), **hack job**, and the **hackney carriage** — still the official licensing term printed on London black cabs.
one_line: Worn stale by overuse — tired, unoriginal, done to death.
root: Hackney (London district; horse kept for hire)
